1000627.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Spanía (“Spain”), from Latin Spānia (“Spain”), a Late Latin and Medieval Latin apheretic form of Latin Hispānia (“Hispania; the Iberian Peninsula”).
The origin of the Latin name is uncertain. It is traditionally derived from Phoenician, from a reconstructed Phoenician or Punic name *ʾī šapān, literally “island of the hyrax”. According to this interpretation, Phoenician speakers mistook the numerous rabbits of the Iberian Peninsula for hyraxes, and the name was understood as “island” or “land of rabbits”. 1004723.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Ullr (“Ull”), with loss of the Old Norse nominative ending -r. The Old Norse theonym is from Proto-Germanic *wulþuz (“glory, splendour”), also continued by Gothic 𐍅𐌿𐌻𐌸𐌿𐍃 (wulþus, “glory, wealth”) and cognate with Latin vultus (“face, countenance; expression”). The name therefore originally meant approximately “the glorious one”.
The related Old Norse divine name Ullinn is preserved in Norwegian place names including Ullensaker and Ullensvang.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Ull, Danish Ull, Swedish Ull and Icelandic Ullur (“Norse god”).
